question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?

sections.title: Signal Generation Mechanism
sections.text: The Pulse-per-Second (PPS) signal is fundamentally an electrical output produced by the GNSS receiver hardware [3]. This pulse is triggered specifically at the moment of each GPS time second change, ensuring that all GPS receivers emit this signal consistently [2]. The generation of this timing reference is not isolated but is part of a broader frequency discipline system. The receiver utilizes an oven-controlled crystal oscillator (OCXO) to generate a stable 10 MHz frequency signal [1]. This oscillator is disciplined to match the frequency of the GNSS signal or atomic standards through a phase-locked loop that employs frequency multiplication [1].

sections.title: Phase and Offset Characteristics
sections.text: While the PPS and the 10 MHz signal are both derived from the GNSS receiver, their exact phase relationship is not inherently defined or guaranteed by the hardware [4]. However, this unknown phase offset is strictly bounded within a range of ±1 nanosecond, which renders the specific phase relationship irrelevant for many high-precision applications [4]. In terms of absolute timing accuracy relative to the true GPS second, the 1PPS signal may exhibit an offset of up to 50 nanoseconds. This deviation highlights the distinction between the internal consistency of the receiver's signals and their alignment with the external GPS time standard.

sections.title: Implications for Clock Bias Re-initialization
sections.text: The provided evidence describes the physical generation of the PPS as a pulse coinciding with GPS time second changes and its relationship to the internal 10 MHz oscillator [3][2][1]. It does not explicitly detail the internal digital control logic or line driver mechanisms used to re-initialize the oscillator offset based on estimated clock bias from Position, Velocity, and Time (PVT) algorithms. The claims confirm that the PPS is generated at second boundaries and that the 10 MHz signal is disciplined by a PLL [2][1], but they do not provide specific information on whether the PPS is physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator that is periodically reset by PVT-derived bias estimates. Therefore, based strictly on the available claims, the specific mechanism of digital re-initialization via PVT bias cannot be confirmed or denied.

question: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?

sections.title: Initialization Strategies and Context
sections.text: The initialization of the embedding layer in transformer models is a critical design choice that influences training dynamics. While deep learning architectures often leverage pre-trained word embeddings to extract comprehensive information from smaller datasets, the standard practice for pre-training large language models frequently involves random initialization [3]. This approach allows the embedding layer to be updated dynamically throughout the training process, rather than relying on static representations derived from external corpora [2]. The decision to use random initialization is often contrasted with the alternative of using pre-trained vectors, such as those from GloVe or word2vec, which can be applied prior to the start of training [1]. This distinction is particularly relevant in the context of the self-supervised pre-training paradigm that has shifted the landscape of transformer-based text processing.

snippets: Prior to training, the embedding layer can be initialized randomly, or initialized by pre-trained embeddings like word2vec [19] or GloVe [21]

We perform experiments with two configurations of the embedding layer: (1) Random, initialized randomly and updated during training, and (2) Pre-trained, initialized by pre-trained representations and updated during training.
At embedding layer, deep learning models make use of pre-trained word embeddings that facilitate them to extract more comprehensive information even from smaller datasets [51].

sections.title: Training Dynamics and Learning Rates
sections.text: The choice of initialization method directly impacts the scheduling of learning rates during the pre-training phase. For models that begin with randomly initialized embeddings, the training protocol typically starts with a maximum learning rate, denoted as η_max, which is then decayed over a specific number of learning steps [5]. This strategy facilitates rapid learning of the embedding matrix without necessitating an additional full training cycle to adjust the initial parameters [5]. In contrast, when models are initialized with pre-trained representations, the learning rate schedule is adjusted to start from half of the maximum value, η_max/2 [4]. This reduction is justified by the fact that both the model weights and the embedding vectors are already reasonably well-trained, requiring less aggressive updates to avoid destabilizing the existing knowledge [4].

snippets: When using pre-initialized models, we start from $\eta_{\mathrm{max}} / 2$ since both the model and embeddings are reasonably well-trained.

During continued pre-training, for models initialized randomly, we begin with $\eta_{\mathrm{max}}$ and decay over $N_{\mathrm{CT}}$ learning steps, allowing quick embedding matrix learning without requiring another full training pass, as is common in language rewiring (Artetxe et al., 2020).

sections.title: Challenges with Pre-trained Embeddings
sections.text: Despite the potential benefits of using pre-trained embeddings, integrating them into the pre-training process presents specific challenges. Adaptations that involve mixing different embedding spaces tend to slow down the convergence of the model [6]. This slowdown is attributed to the complexity involved in selecting the appropriate embedding layers for mixing, which can introduce additional variables that complicate the optimization landscape [6]. Consequently, the simplicity and predictability of random initialization may offer a more stable foundation for the initial stages of pre-training, avoiding the pitfalls associated with aligning disparate pre-trained vector spaces [6].

sections.title: Decoupled Embeddings and Recent Developments
sections.text: Recent research has explored methods to address the limitations of standard embedding layers, such as the decoupled embeddings approach proposed in 2024 [7]. This work, titled "dept: decoupled embeddings for pre-training language models," suggests that separating the embedding mechanisms can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of pre-training [7]. By examining the interplay between random and pre-trained configurations, these studies highlight that the initialization strategy is not merely a technical detail but a fundamental aspect of how models acquire linguistic representations [7]. The ongoing investigation into these methods underscores the importance of understanding why random initialization remains a prevalent baseline, even as new techniques emerge to enhance embedding layer performance [7].

question: For different modulation types like MPSK, QPSK, and MQAM, I'm measuring the error rate but want to understand and measure the Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) more accurately. I'm using a general equation for all modulation types. Is this the right approach, and what should I expect from the EVM vs. Eb/No curve?

sections.title: EVM as a Performance Metric
sections.text: Error Vector Magnitude serves as a critical figure of merit for evaluating signal integrity in digital communications. It is defined as the measure of how far a test signal deviates from a reference signal at the symbol level [2]. This metric is not merely a diagnostic tool but can be considered equivalently useful to traditional metrics such as Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Bit Error Rate (BER) [1]. By establishing relationships among these different performance metrics, researchers have demonstrated that EVM provides a comprehensive view of system performance that aligns with standard industry definitions [1].

sections.title: Applicability Across Modulation Types
sections.text: The user's inquiry regarding the use of a general equation for various modulation types, including MPSK, QPSK, and MQAM, is supported by the derivation of relationships among EVM metrics for different performance indicators [1]. The literature indicates that EVM is a standard industry metric applicable to these common modulation schemes, allowing for consistent comparison across different signal formats [1]. While the specific mathematical derivation for each modulation type is not detailed in the provided claims, the existence of derived relationships suggests that a unified framework for EVM calculation is established in the field [1]. This supports the approach of using a generalized equation, provided it accounts for the specific constellation geometry of the modulation in use [1].

sections.title: Optimization and Estimation Challenges
sections.text: When measuring EVM accurately, particularly in the context of optimizing system parameters, one must account for the mathematical nature of the problem. EVM optimization is generally a non-convex task, which can complicate the search for global minima [2]. To address this, robust estimation of initial conditions for the optimizer is suggested to ensure convergence to accurate results [2]. This implies that simply applying a static equation may not suffice if the measurement setup involves iterative refinement or adaptive filtering, as the non-convex nature of the error surface requires careful initialization [2].

sections.title: Practical Measurement Methodologies
sections.text: In practical applications, EVM measurement can be performed using standard digital Automatic Test Equipment (ATE). For instance, studies have demonstrated the measurement of EVM for RF ZigBee transceivers using such standard digital ATE platforms [3]. This indicates that the measurement of EVM is not restricted to specialized high-end laboratory instruments but can be integrated into standard testing workflows [3]. The use of standard ATE suggests that the underlying principles of EVM calculation are compatible with widely available digital signal processing tools, facilitating broader adoption in both research and industrial settings [3].

sections.title: Expected EVM vs. Eb/No Behavior
sections.text: The relationship between EVM and signal quality is well-documented through comparisons of EVM against SNR and BER. As the signal-to-noise ratio improves, EVM is expected to decrease, reflecting a closer alignment between the received and reference signals [1]. Since Eb/No is a normalized form of SNR, the EVM vs. Eb/No curve should exhibit a similar trend, where higher Eb/No values correspond to lower EVM percentages [1]. The equivalence of EVM to SNR and BER as performance metrics implies that the curve will serve as a reliable predictor of bit error performance, with the specific shape of the curve depending on the modulation type and the noise characteristics of the channel [1].
